title: Chapter 11: Lists: Keeping Many Values in Order
video_title: Python Chapter 11: Lists, Keeping Many Values in Order
summary: The guessing game forgot every guess. Follow Asha as she learns lists: indexes from 0 and from the end, append, insert, remove and pop, slices, building a list in a loop, the in test, and sorted() against sort(). Then watch her build a top three sales line with an AI assistant at all six stages, catching the three smallest sales, an error that never happens and a change of order she did not ask for.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **list** keeps many values in one variable, in a fixed order.
A list of 3 sales and a list of 3,000 sales need the same code.
A playlist, a shopping basket, the messages in a chat: each one is a list.

segments.say: A list keeps many values in one variable, in a fixed order. You can add values, remove them, sort them and go through them one by one.
And a list of 3 sales needs the same code as a list of 3,000.
Your music playlist is a list. So is your shopping basket, and the messages in a chat.

scenes.title: The idea: items with an index
scenes.direction: Teach brackets, indexes from 0 and negative indexes with the diagram. Then mutable versus strings, a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Every item has an index
visual.label: The idea
body: Square brackets, with commas between the items. Counting starts at **0**.

segments.say: A list is written with square brackets, and commas between the items. This list has four items.
Each item has an index: its position. Counting starts at 0. So tea is at index 0, and scone is at index 3.
Negative indexes count from the end. Minus 1 is always the last item, whatever the length of the list.

visual.heading: A list can change
visual.label: The idea
items: Chapter 3: a string cannot be changed after it is made.
A list can: replace an item, add one or remove one.
A list is **mutable**: it can change after it is made.

segments.say: In Chapter 3, you learned that a string cannot be changed after it is made.
A list can. You can replace an item, add one or remove one, and the list itself changes.
We say a list is mutable. It can change after it is made.

visual.question: Which one can you change after it is made?
options: Both a string and a list
visual.explain: A list is mutable. A string cannot be changed after it is made.

segments.say: Quick check. Which one can you change after it is made?

after.say: C. A list. A string cannot be changed. Its methods give you a new string instead.

items: A list keeps many values in order.
Indexes start at 0; minus 1 is the last item.
A list can change after it is made.

scenes.title: Step 2: Change a list

visual.heading: Step 2: Five ways to change a list
visual.label: Build it
rows: Puts `x` at index `i` and moves the rest along.
Removes the first item equal to `x`.
Removes the last item and gives it back.

segments.say: Step 2. A method is a function that belongs to a value, like upper for strings. Lists have methods that change the list itself.
Append adds an item at the end.
Insert puts an item at an index, and moves the rest along.
An index with an equals sign replaces one item.
Remove deletes the first item that matches.
And pop removes the last item, and gives it back to you.

visual.heading: Step 2: The order changes
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Asha's order starts with tea and cake. Line 3 appends a sandwich at the end.
Line 5 inserts juice at index 0, at the front. Everything else moves along by one.
Line 7 replaces the item at index 1 with green tea.

ask.question: Which item does line 7 replace: juice, tea or cake?

after.say: Tea. After line 5, juice is at index 0, so tea moved to index 1.
Line 9 removes cake.
And line 11 pops the last item, sandwich, and keeps it in the variable last. Line 12 prints it, then the shorter list.

scenes.title: Step 3: Slices
scenes.direction: Teach the slice rules first, with the range callback. Ask what line 3 prints, then reveal every line, ending with the slice past the end.

visual.heading: Step 3: A slice takes a part
visual.label: Build it
items: `sales[start:stop]` gives a new list.
It starts at `start` and stops **before** `stop`, like `range()`.
No start: from index 0. No stop: to the end.
A slice never goes past the end. It gives no error.

segments.say: Step 3. A slice takes a part of a list, and gives you a new list. You write a start and a stop, with a colon between them.
It starts at the start index, and stops before the stop index. Exactly like range in Chapter 8.
Leave out the start, and it starts at 0. Leave out the stop, and it goes to the end.
And a slice never goes past the end of the list. It stops there, with no error.

visual.heading: Step 3: Five slices
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Here are five sales. Line 3 slices from 1 to 3.

after.say: 8.0 and 15.75: the items at index 1 and 2. Index 3 is the stop, so it is left out.
Line 4 has no start, so it gives the first two. Line 5 has no stop, so it goes from index 2 to the end.
Line 6 starts at minus 2, so it gives the last two sales.
And line 7 asks for items up to index 10. The list has only five, so the slice stops at the end. No error.

scenes.direction: The fix for the forgetful game. Teach append in a loop, for over a list and in, then ask what line 11 prints.

visual.heading: Step 4: A game that remembers
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

The loop asks three times. Line 5 appends each guess, so the list grows by one item on every pass.
Line 7 goes through the list with for, one item at a time, as it went through a string in Chapter 8.
And the word in checks whether a value is in the list. It gives True or False.

ask.question: The user types 7, 12 and 15. What does line 11 print?

after.say: False. 20 is not one of the guesses.
And the game remembers every guess. Line 6 shows all three.
12 is in the list, so line 10 prints, You tried 12.

scenes.title: Step 5: Sort and add up
scenes.direction: Teach sorted() against sort() with the table first. Ask what line 4 prints, reveal, then sum, min and max. Quiz, then a breather.

segments.say: Step 5. There are two ways to sort a list, and the difference matters.
The function sorted makes a new sorted list. The original list stays the same.
The method sort changes the list itself. And it gives back None, a special value that means no value.

visual.heading: Step 5: sorted() and sort()
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Line 3 prints sorted sales. Line 4 prints sales itself.

after.say: The original order: 12.5, 8.0, 15.75, 9.25. Sorted made a new list, and left sales alone.
Line 5 uses sort, so now the list itself is sorted, smallest first.
Reverse equals True sorts from the biggest to the smallest.
And sum, min and max give the total, the smallest and the biggest number.

visual.question: What does `sales.sort()` give back?
visual.explain: `sort()` changes the list itself and gives back `None`.

segments.say: Quick check. What does the method sort give back?

after.say: A. None. It changes the list itself. The function sorted is the one that gives a new list.

items: `append()`, `insert()`, `remove()`, `pop()` change a list.
A slice stops before its stop index.
`sorted()` makes a new list; `sort()` gives `None`.

segments.say: Back to the mission. Line 2 keeps five sales. Line 3 appends a sixth, 6.50.
Line 4 adds them up with sum. Line 5 counts them with len.
Line 7 divides the total by len, so the average stays right when more sales arrive.

after.say: 21.0 and 15.75, the two biggest sales.
And because line 11 used sorted, not sort, the last line still shows the day in order.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: a worked example
visual.label: Before you start
items: Ask AI to explain a slice or a method with a small list and the exact result.
Run the example yourself. The run decides.
Never paste private data. You are responsible for the code you use.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is the worked example. When AI explains a slice or a method, ask for a small list, the code and the exact result.
Then run the example yourself. And the safety habits from Chapter 1 still apply.

visual.heading: Plan: the steps before the code

messages.text: I am a beginner. My list `sales` holds today's sales in the order they happened. I want a line that shows the three biggest sales, biggest first, and the day order must stay the same. Do not write code yet. List the steps and name the method or function for each.

1. Make a sorted copy, biggest first: `sorted(sales, reverse=True)`.
2. Take its first three items with a slice: `[:3]`.
3. Print them.
4. Print `sales` to check that the day order did not change.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha wants the three biggest sales, biggest first, and the day order must stay the same. She asks for steps, with no code.
The AI's plan: a sorted copy, biggest first. A slice of its first three. Print them. Then print sales, to check the day order.

visual.heading: Write: a worked example of a slice

messages.text: I wrote this line myself. Explain what `sales[:3]` gives, with my list as a worked example. Do not change my code.

`sales[:3]` takes the items at index 0, 1 and 2, in the order of the list: `[12.5, 8.0, 15.75]`.
It does not pick the biggest. It picks the first three.
I ran it. Your example was right:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes a slice herself, and asks the AI to explain it with her own list as a worked example.
The AI says: the first three items, in the order of the list. Not the biggest.
She runs it. The example matches the run.

messages.text: Write code that prints the three biggest sales from my list. Show the exact output.
Here it is. It prints `Top three: [21.0, 15.75, 12.5]`.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for the code, and the exact output.
The AI promises 21.0, 15.75 and 12.5. It sounds completely sure.
Look at line 3. Remember which way sort puts the numbers.

ask.question: The AI says this prints the three biggest sales. Is it right?

after.say: No. Sort puts the smallest first, so the first three items are the three smallest.

segments.say: Asha runs it. 6.5, 8.0 and 9.25: the three smallest sales of the day.

visual.heading: Test: three lists with expected results

messages.text: It printed `[6.5, 8.0, 9.25]`. My check: the first item must equal `max(sales)`, 21.0, so it fails. Fix it, then give me three test lists with the expected output: a normal day, three equal sales and a day with only two sales.

Sort with `reverse=True`, so the biggest comes first.
1. Normal day: `[21.0, 15.75, 12.5]`
2. Equal sales: `[5.0, 5.0, 5.0]`
3. Two sales: an `IndexError`, because the list has fewer than three items.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha shows the AI a check that fails: the first of the top three must equal max, 21.0. Then she asks for a fix and three test lists, each with its expected output.
The fix: reverse equals True. And three expected results. For a day with only two sales, the AI predicts an Index Error.

ask.question: The AI says a day with two sales gives an `IndexError`. Is it right?

after.say: No. Remember step 3: a slice never goes past the end of the list. It stops there, with no error.

visual.heading: Three test lists, on the fixed code

segments.say: Asha runs all three lists. A normal day: 21.0 first, and it equals max. Pass.
Three equal sales: three fives. Pass.
And only two sales: 9.0 and 4.0, with no error.
So the code passes all three tests. But the AI's own expectation for case 3 was wrong. A prediction is not a test. The run is.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I want to keep the day order, so I tried this. I got the error below. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

Line 3 is the cause. `sort()` sorts the list and gives back `None`, so `top` is `None`. Line 4 cannot slice `None`.
The smallest fix: `top = sorted(sales, reverse=True)`.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. The fix sorts sales itself, so the day order is lost. Asha wants to keep it, so she stores the result of sort in a new variable, top. Python stops with a Type Error.
She pastes the code and the full error, and asks for the cause first. The AI names line 3: sort gives back None, and nobody can slice None. The fix is sorted.

visual.heading: The fix: sorted() keeps the day order

segments.say: Asha uses sorted on line 3. The top three are right.
And the day order is still there, on the last line.

messages.text: My top three line works. Suggest one change that makes it shorter or clearer, with one reason. Do not change what it prints.
Drop `reverse=True`: sort normally and take the last three items with `top[-3:]`. It is shorter and shows the same three sales.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one change that makes the line shorter or clearer. And she adds: do not change what it prints.
The AI suggests: sort normally, and take the last three items with a negative slice. It says the output is the same.

visual.heading: Testing the suggestion
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Asha tests it. Line 3 sorts smallest first. Line 4 takes the last three.

ask.question: Asha said: do not change what it prints. Does the suggestion keep that promise?

after.say: No. The same three sales, but in the opposite order: the biggest is now last. The AI ignored her instruction.
A different order is a different output. Asha keeps her sorted version.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 shows the IndexError. Mistake 2 is a spot-it on sort(). Mistake 3 shows remove(). Mistake 4 is the missing comma, then a quiz.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: an index past the end

segments.say: Mistake 1. This list has four items, so its indexes are 0 to 3. Line 3 prints tea.
Line 4 asks for index 4, which does not exist. Python stops with an Index Error: list index out of range.
The fix: the last index is the length minus 1. Or use minus 1.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Line 3 sorts the sales, and stores the result back in sales.

after.say: None. Sort gives back None, so line 3 replaced the whole list with None.
after.heading: Mistake 2: keeping the result of sort()

after.say: The fix: write sales dot sort on its own line, or use sorted.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: removing an item that is not there

segments.say: Mistake 3. The list has tea twice. Line 3 removes only the first tea.
Line 5 removes juice, which is not in the list. Python stops with a Value Error.
The fix: check with in first, and remove only when it is there.
Mistake 4. Line 2 has no comma between tea and cake. Python joins two strings that stand next to each other, so you get one item: teacake.
There is no error, but the list has 2 items, not 3. Check the count with len.

visual.question: A list has 5 items. What is the index of the last item, counting from the start?
visual.explain: Counting starts at 0, so 5 items have the indexes 0 to 4.

segments.say: Quick check. A list has 5 items. What is the index of the last item, counting from the start?

after.say: C. 4. Counting starts at 0, so the indexes are 0 to 4.

items: The last index is the length minus 1.
Never keep the result of `sort()`.
Check with `in` before you remove.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A list keeps many values in order. Indexes start at 0; `-1` is the last item.
A list is mutable: `append()`, `insert()`, `remove()` and `pop()` change it.
A slice `[start:stop]` stops before `stop` and never goes past the end.
`for` goes through a list; `in` checks whether a value is in it.
`sorted()` gives a new list; `sort()` changes the list and gives `None`.
Ask AI for a worked example, then run it yourself.

segments.say: Let's recap. A list keeps many values in order. Indexes start at 0, and minus 1 is the last item.
A list can change: append, insert, remove and pop.
A slice stops before its stop index, and never goes past the end.
For goes through a list, and in checks whether a value is in it.
Sorted gives a new list. Sort changes the list, and gives None.
And with AI: ask for a worked example, then run it yourself.

visual.question: `sales = [3, 9, 1]`. What does `sorted(sales)[-1]` give?
visual.explain: `sorted()` gives `[1, 3, 9]`, and index -1 is its last item, 9.

segments.say: One last check. Sales holds 3, 9 and 1. What does sorted sales, index minus 1, give?

after.say: B. 9. Sorted gives 1, 3, 9, and minus 1 is the last item.
